readerTitle: How KFC ran out of chicken
caseNote: 실제 기업 (KFC UK 2018년 배송 대란, AWS S3 2017년 장애) + 가상 적용 (레스토랑 체인, 소프트웨어 회사)
insight: 위험은 사건이 아니라 구조에서 찾는다. '이것이 내일 멈추면 무엇이 같이 멈추는가'를 물으면 숨은 단일 장애점이 보인다.
misconception: 효율을 위해 한 곳으로 모으는 것은 순수한 이득이다. 백업이 두 개 있으면 안전하다.

sources.text: BBC News and other UK press coverage of the KFC chicken shortage, February 2018
Amazon Web Services, Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region, March 2017

factChecks.note: KFC UK는 2018년 2월 배송 계약을 Bidvest에서 DHL(QSL 협력)로 바꿨고, DHL은 Rugby의 단일 물류센터에서 배송했습니다. 이전 업체가 여러 곳의 창고를 썼다는 점과 정확한 창고 수는 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 'several depots'로만 적었습니다.
폐점 매장 수는 보도마다 다릅니다(수백 곳, 약 900개 매장 중). 카드에는 'hundreds of its roughly 900 UK restaurants'로 적었습니다. 매장 수 약 900개를 확인하세요.
AWS S3 장애(2017년 2월 28일)는 디버깅 중 잘못 입력된 명령으로 예상보다 많은 서버가 제거되며 시작됐다고 AWS 공식 요약에 나옵니다. 영향받은 서비스 범위는 일반적으로만 서술했습니다.
2번·8번 카드의 레스토랑 체인과 소프트웨어 회사는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: How KFC ran out of chicken
body: In February 2018, KFC in the UK had a problem no fried-chicken chain should ever have. It ran out of chicken.
Within days, hundreds of its roughly 900 UK restaurants had closed. The farms were fine. The cooks were fine. One link in the middle was not.

image.label: Empty fried-chicken bucket on a closed restaurant counter
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 불 꺼진 패스트푸드 매장 카운터 위에 빈 치킨 버킷 하나, 문에 'Closed' 팻말. 실제 KFC 로고, 빨간 줄무늬 버킷 디자인, 캐릭터는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: One warehouse or several?
body: You run a chain of 40 restaurants. Deliveries come from three regional warehouses.
A logistics company offers to serve every restaurant from one new central hub. It's cheaper and simpler to manage. What do you do?

options.text: Take the deal. One hub is cheaper and easier to control
options.feedback: You save money every month. But if that hub stumbles, all 40 restaurants stop at once instead of a third of them.

options.text: Take the deal, but keep a backup route ready and switch over gradually
options.feedback: You get most of the savings and still have somewhere to turn if the hub fails. The backup costs a little, like insurance you hope not to use.

options.text: Refuse. Keep all three warehouses forever
options.feedback: Safe, but you pay for three sites every month. A cheaper backup may protect you almost as well.

cards.title: Everything ran through one building.
body: KFC had just moved its UK deliveries to a new logistics partner, DHL. The old supplier had used several depots. The new setup ran from a single distribution centre in Rugby, in central England.
When problems hit that one site in its first days, trucks stopped reaching restaurants across the country. There was no second route to fall back on.
KFC apologised publicly. It took weeks for deliveries to fully recover.

cards.title: Single point of failure
body: A **single point of failure** is one part of a business that, if it stops, stops everything that depends on it.
Notice what made KFC fragile. No single event was unusual. Warehouses have bad weeks. The danger was the *shape* of the system: every restaurant hung from one thread.

image.label: Many restaurants connected to one warehouse by a single line
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 창고 3개가 각자 매장 여러 곳과 연결(하나가 꺼져도 나머지는 불 켜짐). 오른쪽: 창고 1개에 모든 매장이 연결, 창고가 꺼지자 모든 매장이 회색으로. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Ask: if this stopped tomorrow, what stops with it?
body: Single points of failure hide in plain sight. Look for anything you only have one of:
list: **One supplier** for a key ingredient or part
**One site** that handles all orders or production
**One person** who knows how a critical task works
**One customer** who brings in most of your revenue
cards.callout: If the answer is "everything," you've found one.

cards.title: Two of something can still be one.
body: In February 2017, a mistyped command during routine work knocked out a major Amazon Web Services storage system in its Northern Virginia region. Many websites and apps slowed or failed for hours.
Plenty of those businesses had backups and spare servers. But they all sat in the same region. Two copies in one place share one weak spot.
The same goes for two suppliers who buy from the same factory, or two managers trained by the same retiring expert.

cards.title: You can't double everything.
body: Redundancy costs money. A second warehouse, a second supplier or a trained stand-in all add cost and effort every month.
So rank your single points of failure by how bad a failure would be, then protect the worst ones first. And test the backup. A plan nobody has ever used often fails exactly when you need it.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your 12-person software company sells billing tools. Only one engineer, Maya, knows how to release updates and fix the payment system when it breaks.
She's leaving for a three-week holiday next month. What do you do?

options.text: Ask Maya to keep her laptop and stay reachable
options.feedback: It costs nothing today. But you still depend on one person, now tired and far away, and she may not answer in time.

options.text: Have Maya write down the steps and walk a colleague through a real release before she goes
options.feedback: It takes a few days of her time, but now two people can do the job, and the written steps outlast the holiday.

options.text: Hire a contractor to cover while she's away
options.feedback: Someone is on call, but without Maya's knowledge they may not know the system. Knowledge needs to be shared before it can be covered.

cards.title: Find the one thing everything depends on.
body: Risk often lives in the shape of your business, not in rare events. Spot what you have only one of, then protect the parts whose failure would hurt most.
**Try it today:** list five things your business can't run without. Circle any you have only one of. Pick one and plan a backup.
